title: Responsive design
canDo: make layouts adapt to any screen size

sources.name: Kevin Powell — Conquering Responsive Layouts (free course)

blocks.md: Your page has to look right on a phone *and* a giant monitor. Responsive design is how one layout adapts to any screen — and it's a skill that instantly makes your work look professional.

blocks.canDo: make layouts adapt to any screen size

blocks.md:
**What to focus on:**

- **Mobile-first**: write your base styles for small screens, then *add* styles for bigger screens.
- **Media queries**: `@media (min-width: 700px) { ... }` applies rules only above a certain width.
- Relative units (`%`, `rem`, `fr`) over fixed pixels so things can flex.
- The viewport `<meta>` tag (you'll see it on every page).

The big mindset shift: don't design for one screen and patch the rest — start simple and enhance.

blocks.label: ▶ Do this: Kevin Powell's free "Conquering Responsive Layouts" — a 21-day mini-course, one short challenge a day. The daily-bite format is perfect for building the habit.
📖 MDN's responsive-design page for the reference version of media queries and units.

blocks.md: Test responsiveness by dragging your browser window narrow/wide, or open dev tools (F12) and toggle the device toolbar. Watch where the layout breaks — that's where a media query goes.

questions.question: In a mobile-first workflow, which type of media query do you use to apply styles for larger screens?
questions.explanation: Mobile-first means base styles target small screens, and `min-width` queries layer on enhancements as the viewport grows wider.

questions.question: What does the `<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">` tag do?
options: It sets the page background color on mobile browsers
It tells the browser to match the layout width to the device screen width instead of using a desktop-sized virtual viewport
It disables zooming on touchscreen devices permanently
It loads a separate mobile stylesheet automatically
questions.explanation: Without this tag, mobile browsers render the page at a wide virtual viewport and then scale it down, breaking responsive layouts.

questions.question: Why are relative units like `rem`, `%`, and `fr` preferred over fixed `px` values in responsive layouts?
options: They render faster than pixel values on modern GPUs
They scale with the user's settings or the container size, so layouts adapt naturally to different screens
Browsers ignore `px` units on mobile devices
They automatically add media queries to your stylesheet
questions.explanation: Relative units flex with the viewport or parent container, reducing the number of breakpoints needed and making layouts inherently more adaptable.
